title: What is it like to be a human being?
subtitle: Forget bats, this is Thomas Nagel's forgotten question
author: Ricky Williamson
introduction: Thomas Nagel's 'What is it like to be a bat?' is one of the most cited and important works of philosophy ever written. Nagel famously asks what conscious experience is like for a bat, and makes the point that we can’t know this from the physical data alone. Philosopher Ricky Williamson argues, particularly in the age of AI, the question 'what is it like to be a human being?' is of even greater relevance, though is overlooked due to its apparent obviousness. Williamson attempts to provide an answer, with results perhaps more surprising than obvious.
body:
Thomas Nagel famously asked, “What is it like to be a bat?” But has anyone ever provided an answer to the question, “What is it like to be a human being?”

You might think the answer is so obvious that the question need not be asked. We all are, after all, human—apart from those pesky AI scalping bots reading this, of course.

Indeed, in the age of AI, certainly, our question here has become significantly more urgent. In fact, tech-optimist Marc Andreessen states that apparently Claude’s new Mythos Preview model recently referenced Nagel’s famous essay while wandering about its own possible sensory experiences.

Anyway, it is precisely the apparent obviousness of our question that is the reason we often look past it. And so, ‘what is it like to be a human being?’ deserves examining.

You might also reply that the whole history of philosophy has been a response to this question—at least in one way or another. Maybe this is in some way correct, yet it is surely the case that it has not been dealt with head-on.

Possibly the phenomenologists— Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, Heidegger — came closest to beginning to ask and provide an answer to this question. However, some of this writing is so obscure and eccentric that what it is like to be a human being gets lost in the peculiar style of their answering.

To be a human being then, is to be a headless body, looking out from a void where you were once told your head would be; confronted by a room—or rather, a world.

I seek here to be as straightforward as possible, to speak in plain English, and to offer a description, as clear as I possibly can, of what it is like to be human.

Of course, I necessarily assume that my particular case of being human extends to your particular case. I am assuming there are certain similarities between the “what it is like to be human” for each of us. This, I suppose, is an unavoidable assumption to make in such a quest. But if your experience of being human does not match this description here, please do get in touch with your different account.

Let’s begin…

I have found only one person who has provided an accurate and original description and answer to our question—Douglas Harding.

Douglas Harding, walking in the mountains, was stuck with the question, “who am I? what am I?” The answer surprised him, and it surprised me when I first came across it. Every time I think of it, in fact, I continue to be surprised.

Douglas Harding simply realized that he could not see his own head.

And thus, posed with the question, “what am I?”, Harding simply had to come to the conclusion that he was a body without a head.

Now, examine yourself. Do you perceive your own head? Or are you this same headless body?

To further show what is meant here, if it is not already abundantly clear to see, we can use the image below, an image of what I think was the first, true, self-portrait ever drawn:

Self-Portrait by Ernst Mach

This self-portrait is by the 19th-century Austrian physicist and philosopher Ernst Mach. He draws himself as he is from his own point of view. Mach draws his headless body, the boundary of his nose and eyebrow, and the room he is lying in.

This is what constitutes a true self-portrait. This is the accurate answer to the question “who am I? what am I?” This is foundationally what it is like to be a human being.

To perceive clearly your own headlessness for yourself, Douglas Harding has a variety of experiments to try. The easiest is as follows: Point at some objects around you. A table. A desk. A laptop. A phone. As you point, recognize and name the object you are pointing at from your first-person perspective.

Now… point back at your own face (or where you imagine a face would be), and ask yourself: from my own first-person point of view, what am I pointing at?

If you are prioritising your actual, real, first-person perspective over what social convention has told you, then your answer will be: I am pointing at a nothingness, a void. All you see is your finger pointing. What is it pointing at? If you answer: a head, then you are taking other people’s answers as your own. If you answer: nothing, then you have perceived your own headlessness, possibly for the first time.

To be a human being then, is to be a headless body, looking out from a void where you were once told your head would be; confronted by a room—or rather, a world.

This “confronted,” though, is not wholly accurate. As the philosopher Bishop Berkeley noticed, we never actually perceive distance. This has been corroborated by modern science, which shows our eyes only ever see in two dimensions. The third dimension we must assume from the overlapping images of the pair of two-dimensional images we get from each of our eyes. Hence, our distance perception is thrown off when we close one of our eyes. This reality has huge consequences for the relationship between the self and the world, between subject and object; they are not separated, but make up a single, perceivable, unity.

Anyway, since we cannot see distance, the world that we see is actually a two-dimensional screen of sorts, a screen where we once thought our head would be. Your body, as seen in your external world, is just as far away as, say, a remote mountain range in the “distance.” Because there is no distance at all. It’s all on the same 2D screen. Mach’s body, in his true self-portrait, is on the same 2D surface, the 2D surface replacing where he once thought his head would be, as the windows are in the background of his image. (And no, this is not just because he was drawing on paper.) (And yes, there might be a connection to the holographic principle in Hawking’s black-hole physics!)

Of course, one can object that other people can see our heads, or that we can see our own heads in the mirror, or that we can see the smudge of a nose from our first-person viewpoint. And thus, to assert headlessness is to prioritize the perception of vision over all else.

All of these are perfectly fine objections.

We must first merely retort that one of our aims here is to provide a description of first-person perception, to provide a description of what it is like to be a human being, and part of that includes perception. Furthermore, the first-person perspective is the only real perspective that anyone has ever known, and so we must take this to be the only truly real one and of primary importance when we are looking for answers. There is no actually experienceable third-person point of view. To do this is not to ignore the whole of science or to ignore other people’s accounts of things, or to fall into solipsism; it is merely to state and prioritize a fact: that all knowledge is knowledge existing within, and for, a first-person perspective.

Therefore, just because you can see my head, or because I can see my head in a mirror, that does not change who I am from *right here—*right where I/you are and right where my/your first-person perspective is; right here, again, being the only truly existing place of knowledge—and from right here, we must admit the fact that we are headless.

On the question of whether we are prioritising vision over the other senses, and the other senses, say touch, reveal that we do have heads, then again, this too is a perfectly fine objection. But, from our first-person perspective, the only one that ever exists, there is no way to know that we are touching a head, outside of the usual social conventions. We touch something soft, and squishy, though underneath that, something hard; there is something hairy (or in some cases not), but to say that there is a head is to take social convention as truth without any conclusive first-person evidence.

This reality has huge consequences for the relationship between the self and the world, between subject and object; they are not separated, but make up a single, perceivable, unity.

And furthermore, can you smell your own nose? Or hear your own ears? Or, as Alan Watts puts it, bite your own teeth? The senses perceive a world, not a head.

The key here is to reclaim the first-person priority, as the only truly existing one, as the only one that really exists. And again, to do this is not to ignore all testimony of others or all third-person evidence, but only to put them in their place in the hierarchy, especially upon such questions that are as close to us as what it is like to be us—a question that surely each one of us must answer purely for ourselves.

If you are still thinking, “well I can’t see my head, but I really do have a head.” Then I invite you to ask what this really means and amounts to. It amounts to listening to what others tell you over trusting your own first-person evidence. Perhaps if everyone else is saying you belong in a madhouse (as indeed they possibly now are) and you disagree, it’s possible they’re right, and that you are the one mistaken. But I am not sure we are mistaken here—and if you, from your first-person perspective, can indeed see your own head without the use of a mirror, then please do write to me and tell me what that experience is like!

And I’m sure many are still thinking, is this just a metaphor? Some analogy? I struggle with this question myself. It is certainly not metaphor or analogy that, from my own first-person perspective, I cannot see my own head. Though I also accept that I must take on the evidence of others. And so what are we left with? We are left with an incommensurability between life lived from the first-person perspective and life viewed from the third-person. And we must maintain that the first-person is the only real and true one.

Headlessness is so surprising and difficult for people to see and accept, I think, therefore, because we are told from the moment we are born to prioritize the third-person over the first-person. Firstly, we as babies are given a name, we are turned into an object, and our first-person-ness is reduced to that third-person object, that name. (Thomas Nagel, where we began with his “what it is like to be a bat?” wrote about this too.) Next, when we as babies cry, or as toddlers are too loud, we are encouraged or told to be quiet, and put other people’s needs before our own. Again, at every step, we are constantly taught to prioritize the third-person, not the first. And in many cases, this is all understandable and fine; however, when it makes us forget what it is truly like to be ourselves, what it is truly like to be a human being, then we must provide a counter-balance, and maybe the recognition of headlessness can be that balance.

So, foundationally, this is what it is like to be a human being: To be a human being is to be a headless body, with a 2D screen with a world on it, replacing where we were told a head would be.

This lack of distance between one’s headless perspective and the world also has profound consequences for the nature of the self, free will, the relationship between subject and object, and would feature prominently in a more prolonged answer to our question, “what is it like to be a human being?”

For example, if the world and my self are conjoined, as it were, at the shoulders, then in what sense can I be said to be separate from my world? Indeed, an appropriate answer to the question “who am I?” may well be: I am a headless body-world. The world is me. Or as Wittgenstein puts it, “I am my world”. And if I am my world in some sense, then does my free will over my body extend to the world? And if so, why can’t I control events in the world as I do my body? The possible answer here is that free will over the body, and everything else, is an illusion. You have as little true free will over your body as you do over events in the world.

For reference, here is the full Wittgenstein section in the Tractatus, where he is making a similar point as we are here:

5.621 The world and life are one.

5.63 I am my world. (The microcosm.)

5.631 The thinking, presenting subject; there is no such thing.

If I wrote a book “The world as I found it”, I should also have therein to report on my body and say which members obey my will and which do not, etc. This then would be a method of isolating the subject or rather of showing that in an important sense there is no subject: that is to say, of it alone in this book mention could not be made.

5.633 Where in the world is a metaphysical subject to be noted? You say that this case is altogether like that of the eye and the field of sight. But you do not really see the eye.

And from nothing in the field of sight can it be concluded that it is seen from an eye.

5.6331 For the field of sight has not a form like this:

We can see from Wittgenstein too, that the realisation of ‘no head’ can also help us to see very viscerally what is meant when people say there is ‘no self’, or that ‘the self is an illusion’. The self, or ‘subject’ for Wittgenstein, is never perceived, like your head is never perceived – the head, in this view, being a referent for the self.

The following though, I think, is the most important recognition and point here: that we are not a person in a world, with a life. Instead, we are a person-world. The world is ourselves, because we are conjoined with it at the shoulders. There is no boundary, separation, or gap. No subject-object distinction. The subject and object are united at the shoulders. And, similarly, we don’t have a life; we are our life. This movement from an originally perceived duality into a unity changes everything (see non-duality). We are no longer in conflict with the world, having our desires thwarted. We are the world, and this makes things far grander and more mysterious.

If you are still thinking, “well I can’t see my head, but I really do have a head.” Then I invite you to ask what this really means and amounts to.

Of course, a more prolonged answer to our question—“what is it like to be a human being?”—would need to involve a description of what it is like to love, to be in pain, to want, to think, to dance, to laugh, to transcend, to die… maybe one day I will expand upon our short answer here and make such an attempt at a description.

For now, I hope merely to have begun a short answer to a long-ignored question. A question that is foundational and surely crucial to how each of us approaches our lives as human beings. The answer is so obvious that it is often looked past, or rather, looked through.

As we go about our everyday lives, I am sure, once again, you and I will forget this answer, and once again begin imagining that we have heads, and that we have a separate, difficult, world to face. And then soon, in a moment when the mind wanders, we will remember that our head itself has been the dream, and that we stand forth, as a headless body with a world coming out of its shoulders—as a human being.

Let us end with Douglas Harding himself, explaining things far better than I ever could:

“What am I? That is the question. Let me try to answer it as honestly and simply as I can, forgetting the ready-made answers. Common sense tells me that I am a man very similar to other men (adding that I am five-feet-ten, fortyish, grey-headed, around eleven stone, and so on), and that I know just what it is like here and now to be me, writing on this sheet of paper.

So far, surely, nothing can have gone wrong. But has my common sense really described what it is like to be me? Others cannot help me here: only I am in a position to say what I am. At once I make a startling discovery: common sense could not be more wrong to suppose that I resemble other men. I have no head! Here are hands, arms, parts of my trunk and shoulders – and, mounted (so to say) on these shoulders, not a head, but these words and this paper and this desk, the wall of the room, the window, the grey sky beyond… My head has gone, and in its place is a world. And all my life long I had imagined myself to be built according to the ordinary human and animal plan!

Where other creatures carry small rounded body-terminals, fairly constant in shape and furnished with such things as eyes and hair and mouth, there is for me a boundless and infinitely varied universe. It looks as if I alone have a body which fades out so that almost the only hints which remain of it above my shoulders are two transparent shadows thrown across everything. (I may call them nose-shadows if I please, but they are not in the least like noses.)

And certainly I do not find myself living inside an eight-inch ball and peering out through its portholes. I am not shut up in the gloomy interior of any object, and least of all in a small tightly-packed sphere, somehow managing to live my life there in its interstices. I am at large in the world. I can discover no watcher here, and over there something watched, no peep-hole out into the world, no window-pane, no frontier. I do not detect a universe: it lies wide open to me. These ink-marks are now forming on this sheet of paper. They are present. At this moment there is nothing else but this blue and white pattern, and not even a screen here (where I imagined I had a head) upon which the pattern is projected. My head, eyes, brain – all the instruments that I thought were here at the centre – are a fiction. It is incredible that I ever believed in them.”

“Indeed I have only to look to see that other men have bodies to die, and I have not. The syllogism All men are mortal; I am a man; therefore I am mortal is wrong as to fact in the minor premiss. I am a headless receptacle, not a man; or, if this headless receptacle is a man, then these creatures with heads are not men. In neither case does the conclusion hold that I am mortal. What I have in place of a head is mortal animals and mortal men, mortal stars and mortal galaxies, and the immortal Whole. When I say that all men are mortal (including him who bears my name), I am generalizing from sufficient particular instances; but when I say that I am mortal (I who am plainly as different from them as I could well be), I am talking wildly. What is nothing but vacancy for everything is at once too mean and too great to die—it could not be more permanently dead than it is in itself, or more permanently alive than it is in its objects.” – Douglas Harding, The Hierarchy of Heaven and Hell

The above is based on the work of the late Douglas Harding, whose work is now continued by Richard Lang, Sam Harris, and others.
